5187.dq: Where intonation allows it, stress occurs on the first syllable of two syllable words and the second syllable of longer words.
5187.dloc: OPD p. 2 (running header 'Printed: September 1, 2004 Page 2'), section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', the single sentence between the Vowels section and 'Syllable Patterns' of; long-vowel statement at the head of the Vowels section on the same page.- with p. 2.
5187.heavy: The OPD does not use the word 'weight': it counts vowels. 'Long vowels are interpreted as sequences of two vowels' and the Syllable Patterns table splits every vowel sequence into separate syllables (o'.no.u, da.ka.na.a, to.o.va, o.o.an.sing), so a long vowel contributes two counting units to the 'first/second syllable' rule; coda consonants (VC, CVC, N syllable types) contribute nothing, because the rule is a pure count over these vowel-syllables. This is the mora-counting system the catalog's naas1242 record codes as CVV (Brown 2025: long vowels bimoraic, codas weightless).
5187.dflt: Second syllable in words of three or more syllables; first syllable in two-syllable words (all syllables light = short vowels).
5187.prule: Positional, non-contrastive word stress counted over vowels from the left edge: on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables and on the first syllable of two-syllable words, where 'syllable' in this sheet is one vowel (long vowels are 'sequences of two vowels' and are syllabified as two syllables: to.o.va, da.ka.na.a). Read against conventional syllabification that is the peninitial-mora rule the catalog already holds for Naasioi [naas1242] from Brown 2025: stress the second vowel-mora of the word, so the first syllable if it has a long vowel, otherwise the second syllable; bivocalic (bimoraic) words stress the first vowel (final avoidance); codas (VC, CVC, syllabic-N syllable types are listed) play no part in the rule. Stress yields to intonation ('Where intonation allows it'). One stress per word; no secondary stress mentioned. Hurd & Hurd 2020 [1970] sec. 2, p. 2 states the same placement and adds 'Stress is nonphonemic. With words in isolation...'.

5187.tone: The OPD heading reads 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' but the sheet says nothing about tone; 'stress' occurs only in this one sentence. Rausch 1912 p. 107 (Nasioi of the Kieta/Koromira mission area) describes a 'dynamischer Akzent' with a pitch realization (in words of three or more syllables accented on the second or third syllable, that syllable and all preceding ones are 'hochtonig', the following ones 'tieftonig'), says many disyllables have both syllables at the same pitch level with very weak stress, and treats accent as meaning-distinguishing (kara 'Liebe' vs kara 'Mond', dupui pairs). Later Hurd work and Brown 2025 treat stress as nonphonemic; Rausch's pairs are plausibly unmarked vowel-length differences. Not a tone language in any later description.

tn.quote: Il existe deux catégories de tons: tons simples et tons complexes. Bakel Soninke (Senegal), by contrast, shows 'des réalisations prosodiques très différentes' and may be losing its tone system (p. 28); that remark concerns Bakel, not Sillanka.

5199.dq: Lukas 1953:7 as quoted in Dybo 1995:239: 'Die Tubusprache besitzt einen starken Akzent (Druck), der der Sprache einen energischen Charakter verleiht. In welcher Weise der Akzent rhythmisch im Satz verteilt wird, bedarf näherer Untersuchung.' - neither Lukas nor Tucker & Bryan say whether the accent is a word-level or a sentence-level prominence.
5199.dloc: Dybo, V. A. 1995 (Moskovskij lingvisticheskij zhurnal 1: 236-279), p. 239, second paragraph: Lukas, J. 1953, Die Sprache der Tubu in der zentralen Sahara, p. 7, quoted in German after 'О системе тонов в Тубу и его акценте Й. Лукас пишет следующее:' and closed '[Lukas 1953, S.7]'. Tucker & Bryan 1966, p. 170, sec. 2 'Tone and Stress' relays the same remark as "a strong 'Akzent (Druck)' in TUBU" without naming a unit.
5199.prule: No word-stress rule stated for Teda. The chapter reports (after Le Cœur 1956) that Teda, unlike Kanuri, has no elaborate tonal system and that Le Cœur leaves tone unmarked; for Tubu (Lukas's southern/Kashirda material) it reports important but fluctuating tone with lexical and grammatical uses, High/Low/Rising tones, and a strong stress accent ('Akzent (Druck)') that Lukas mentions but does not illustrate and that may affect tones; vowel length in Teda-Tubu is 'perhaps associated with stress'. Where stress falls in the word is not stated by Tucker & Bryan, nor by Lukas as quoted in Dybo 1995:239 ('In welcher Weise der Akzent rhythmisch im Satz verteilt wird, bedarf näherer Untersuchung'), and Dybo 1995:240 states that Lukas accents every example 'не давая, впрочем, какого-либо общего правила, которое определяло бы место ударения в словоформе' (without, however, giving any general rule that would fix the place of stress in the word-form).
5199.srule: Not mentioned in Tucker & Bryan 1966, ch. 9 sec. 2 'Tone and Stress' (p. 170) and sec. 1a (p. 168); not mentioned in Dybo 1995 (pp. 239-240, 263, 269), whose analysis marks and derives a single accent per word-form.

5201.dq: En la jerarquía prosódica del cuicateco, la formación de la palabra fonológica tiene como requerimiento que el pie métrico tenga un contenido mínimo de dos moras y que el acento se fije en la segunda mora de derecha a izquierda según la exposición de Martínez y Mendoza (2016). (p. 47) — stress is assigned in the formation of the phonological word ('palabra fonológica', example (1) p. 19 lists 'as…
5201.dloc: sec. 2.4 p. 47; with example (1) p. 19 (sec. 1.3, 'palabra fonológica... asignación de acento') and sec. 6.4 p. 146 ('los radicales').
5201.heavy: A syllable containing the second mora from the right edge of the root; heaviness = a long (bimoraic) vowel (San Giacomo 2017 p. 97 [βi⁴ˈkuː³] 'fiesta', [jų³ˈðuː⁴] 'llano' vs [ˈka²ka²] 'papel', [ˈjuː⁴ði⁴] 'elote'; San Giacomo 2025 p. 46 [ðu³ˈtuː³⁴] 'hill': 'it falls on the last syllable of the word 'hill' because the vowel is long and the second mora, counted from the right to the left, is found in this syllable'). The mora is the tone-bearing unit ('En cuicateco la unidad portadora de tono es la mora', p. 47); the phonological word requires a foot of at least two moras ('un contenido mínimo de dos moras', p. 47), so monosyllabic roots lengthen (ˈnãː 'cara' p. 19; Teotilálpam [ˈⁿdoː⁴²⁴] 'vena' Cuadro 6.4, [ˈtʃãː⁴] 'lune' Cuadro 6.5). Codas: the thesis's 'prohibición de coda' (p. 145) is stated for the colonial Confessonario variety only ('Las sílabas fonológicas del cuicateco del Confessonario podían ser CV o V... iii) la prohibición de coda'); present-day varieties have VC/CVC syllables (San Giacomo 2017 p. 97: 'permite dos consonantes asignadas al onset y una en coda... (Ariano 2016): V, VC, CV, CCV y CVC'; San Giacomo 2025 p. 46 citing Ariano 2023; Mendoza's Teotilálpam [ˈsnĩŋ³⁴] ~ [ˈsⁿdẽŋ³⁴] 'sombrero', Cuadro 6.4 p. 125, a stressed CVC monosyllable printed without a length mark where Tepeuxila [ˈsⁿdĩː⁴³⁴] and Reyes Pápalo [ˈsnĩː³²³] have long vowels). Whether a coda consonant carries a mora is unstated in every source read, so CVC weight is neither asserted nor excluded. Whether a laryngeal feature (CVʔ) carries a mora is left open for the colonial variety (p. 146: 'ya sea con valor de una mora o, como sucede en algunas realizaciones actuales, entre la transición moraica').
5201.dflt: Penultimate syllable of the root (the first syllable of a disyllabic short-vowelled root: [ˈka²ka²] 'papel', ˈkʷekuð); a monosyllabic root is lengthened to two moras and stressed (ˈnãː 'cara').
5201.prule: Weight-sensitive, non-contrastive: a moraic trochee at the right edge of the root. Stress falls on the syllable that contains the second mora counting from the right edge of the root ('la sílaba de la segunda mora a partir del linde derecho [de] los radicales'; 'el acento se fije en la segunda mora de derecha a izquierda'). A root whose final syllable has a long (bimoraic) vowel is stressed on that final syllable; a root with short vowels is stressed on its penultimate syllable; monosyllabic roots are lengthened to satisfy the two-mora minimum of the phonological word and carry the stress (p. 19: nã 'cara' -> ˈnãː; ku+eku+ði 'IRRE-llorar=2PS' -> ˈkʷekuð). Prefixes and enclitics lie outside the counting domain (corpus forms a-ti-ˈβaʔ=ði, tʃe-noɣiˈβiʔ=ði, ˈβiʔ=ði). Stated for 'las variedades actuales de cuicateco' in general; illustrated by San Giacomo 2017 for San Juan Tepeuxila: [βi⁴ˈkuː³] 'fiesta', [jų³ˈðuː⁴] 'llano' (final long vowel, final stress) vs [ˈka²ka²] 'papel', [ˈjuː⁴ði⁴] 'elote'.
5201.srule: Not mentioned in Mendoza Hernández 2023 (sec. 6.4 'Características prosódicas' pp. 145-146, sec. 2.4 p. 47, sec. 1.3 pp. 19-20 read): the thesis describes a single stress per root (a moraic trochee at the right edge of the root) and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress; the cross-check sources for San Juan Tepeuxila (San Giacomo 2017 pp. 97-98; San Giacomo 2025 p. 46) are likewise silent.

The thesis analyses the colonial Confessonario and compares it with present-day speech from 8 communities in INALI's three variants: centro (Santos Reyes Pápalo, San Juan Tepeuxila, San Lorenzo Pápalo, San Sebastián Tlacolula), norte…
5201.exq_: La asignación del acento suele coincidir con la sílaba prominente en palabras bisilábicas o de mayor extensión. (p. 146) — the only hedge; it concerns the coincidence of the stressed syllable with the 'sílaba prominente' (the syllable licensing the most oppositions), not exceptions to the mora rule…
5201.tone: Cuicatec is tonal ('el cuicateco es tonal', p. 47); the tone-bearing unit is the mora, and tones associate one-to-one or one-to-many with moras (p. 47, citing Needham & Davis 1946 and San Giacomo 2017: four level, five contour, three complex tones for Tepeuxila). Stress is described independently of tone as the position licensing the most segmental oppositions, with intensity and duration as correlates (p. 146). No pitch-accent analysis.

tn.quote: Al igual que los otros integrantes de la familia otomangue, el cuicateco es tonal. … En cuicateco la unidad portadora de tono es la mora (Needham y Davis 1946 y San Giacomo 2017); y su asociación ocurre entre un tono y una mora, o bien entre un tono y varias moras. … De acuerdo con los estudios publicados el paradigma de tonos varía entre los tres y cuatro registros de nivel. … Anderson y Concepción (1983), también para Santa María, y San Giacomo (2017) para Tepeuxila han hallado cuatro alturas tonales; en este último San Giacomo propone además cinco patrones de contorno y 3 patrones complejos
tn.translation: Like the other members of the Otomanguean family, Cuicatec is tonal. … In Cuicatec the tone-bearing unit is the mora (Needham & Davis 1946; San Giacomo 2017), and association holds between one tone and one mora, or between one tone and several moras. … According to the published studies the tone paradigm varies between three and four level registers. … Anderson & Concepción (1983), also for Santa María, and San Giacomo (2017) for Tepeuxila have found four tone heights; in the latter San Giacomo further proposes five contour patterns and 3 complex patterns
tn.cite: Mendoza Hernández, Diego. 2023. Representación y sonido en la escritura de un confesionario bilingüe español-cuicateco colonial. Tesis de licenciatura, Facultad de Filosofía y Letras, UNAM (asesora Marcela San Giacomo). 223 pp. TESIUNAM hdl:20.500.14330/TES01000850266.
tn.locator: sec. 2.4 'Estudios lingüísticos previos', p. 47 with Cuadro 6
tn.note: Tonal; the mora bears tone. Varieties: 3 or 4 level tones; Tepeuxila 4 level, 5 contour, 3 complex (12). A bare high tone can mark 1st person. Stress is separate: 2nd mora from the root's right edge.

5201.cfw: Mendoza Hernández (2023), who collected data in eight Cuicatec communities including the Teutila towns of San Pedro Teutila, Santa María Tlalixtac and San Andrés Teotilálpam, and San Giacomo (2017, 2025) for San Juan Tepeuxila place stress on the syllable that holds the second mora counted from the right edge of the root, while the older Pápalo descriptions (Anderson & Concepción Roque 1983; Needham & Davis 1946) speak of a light stress at the beginning of the root, which picks out the same syllable in ordinary CVCV and CVː roots, so the sources differ in formulation rather than in where stress falls; no published description treats the stress of Teutila Cuicatec on its own.

qtr.text: [p.57] Apart from a few languages such as Swahili, almost all Bantu languages are tone languages, and most have phonological tone (Kisseberth and Odden 2003: 59). Like the great majority of Bantu languages, Bende has distinctive tone that differentiates meaning. ... [p.59] There are three stem/root tonal types, called H(igh), L(ow) and 0 type: H type begins with H, L type begins with L, and in the 0 type the penultimate syllable is H and the final syllable L again. Most loanwords are realised as 0 type. ... Tone rule 1, basic realised tones of stems/roots [1σ 2σ 3σ 4σ+]: H type H HH HHH HHHH …

5202.dq: No stress at any level is described. The tonal melody is computed over the word: [p.59] 語幹ないし語根ごとに決められた声調型で実現されるべき H ないし L は, 語全体の音節数によって H や L の声調を 1 つずつ音節に結びつけられないことがある. そうした場合, 1 音節上で HL が F, LH が R で実現される.
5202.dloc: p.59 (第3章 声調, §1.2 声調の種類, 声調型), p.3
5202.prule: No stress rule is stated. The thesis describes a lexical tone system: each noun stem / verb root belongs to one of three tonal types (H, L, 0) and the surface tones H/L/F/R are assigned by tonal type and the word's syllable count (声調規則 1: H type H/HH/HHH/HHHH, L type R/LH/LHH/LHHH, 0 type R/RL(or HL)/LHL/LLHL; most loans are 0 type).
5202.quote: [p.57] Swahili 語など少数の言語を除き, ほとんどの Bantu 諸語は声調言語で, その多くが音韻的声調を持つ(Kisseberth and Odden 2003: 59). ベンデ語も大多数の Bantu 諸語と同様, 意味の区別に弁別的な声調を持つ. ... [p.59] 語幹ないし語根の声調型には 3 種類あり, それぞれ H(igh) 型, L(ow) 型, 0 型と呼ぶことにする. H 型は語幹ないし語根が H で始まるもの, L 型は語幹ないし語根が L で始まるもの, 0 型は後ろから 2 番目の音節が H となり最終音節は再び L となるものである. 借用語の多くが 0 型で実現される. ... 声調規則 1 語幹, 語根の基本的な実現声調 [1σ 2σ 3σ 4σ以上 例(2σ語根)]: H 型 H HH HHH HHHH -bhá.mbá (皮を)張る; L 型 R LH LHH LHHH -bha.ndá 突っつく; 0 型 R RL/HL LHL LLHL -soó.ka 降りる.
5202.loc: p.57 (第3章 声調, §1 ベンデ語声調の特徴) and p.59 (§1.2 声調の種類, 声調型; 声調規則 1); also p.269 (終章 §2 方言差), p.7 (序章 §1.5 + fn.3), p.20 (第1章, (3) トングウェ語の特徴, after Guthrie 1967-71 vol.2: 47). TUFS repository scans (image-only): pp.1, 3; p.3; p.7; p.4.
5202.idn: The cited thesis is a description of Bende (Guthrie F.12; Glottolog bend1258, a separate catalog record) from fieldwork in Mpanda District. It bears on Tongwe (F.11) through the author's explicit statement that Bende and Tongwe are two dialects of one language, identical 'including tone' (p.269), which rests on her…
5202.exq_: No stress rule, so no stress exceptions. On the tone rule: [p.59] 音節構造や統語構造により異形があるが, 異形については後述する. [p.59] 借用語の多くが 0 型で実現される.
5202.tone: Distinctive lexical tone ([p.57] minimal pairs íikálá 'clawless otter' vs íikalá 'charcoal', lúsángá 'flower' vs lúsangá 'healer's maracas', úughwě 'you' vs uúghwe 'this (proximal demonstrative)'; verbs kúfúlá / kúfulá / kufuúla). Surface tones H, L, F, R realised on short-vowel, long-vowel, diphthong and glide+vowel syllables alike (table (4), p.59). Three stem/root tonal types H, L, 0 with melodies fixed by syllable count (声調規則 1). Tongwe-specific tone evidence in the thesis: Guthrie's characterisation of F.11 Tongwe, quoted on p.20 under '(3) トングウェ語の特徴': 'Tones: Fully distinctive, but opaque'; Guthrie's zone-F feature 16 on the same page: 'F.33 (Laŋgi)を除き, すべての言語で語彙的声調が用いられる. 声調によって時制が区別される例が多い.'; and the tone-marked Tongwe forms in the p.269 dialect-difference table (íibhíngá, mábhíngá; síinyú, fíinyú; mumbáti, mimbáti; muunyú; kabhěnga, tubhěnga; síkólé, fíkólé). The words アクセント / 強勢 / stress / accent occur on none of the pages (pp.7, 20, 57, 59, 269) nor, on a sweep of ch.2 §1, ch.3 §§2-4 and the English/Japanese abstracts, elsewhere. Bende long vowels are lexical or arise from vowel concatenation (Hyman 2003 types a-b), not from penultimate lengthening (p.30).

tn.translation: [p.58] In Bende, tone is not a matter of H or L being fixed for each syllable of the word; the tonal type is fixed for the stem or root as a whole. The tones realised phonetically are determined by which tonal type the stem or root belongs to and by how many syllables the whole word has. There are four phonetic tones: high H, low L, falling F, rising R. ... [p.59] The four phonetic tones H, L, F, R can be realised on a syllable, but F is HL and R is LH realised on one syllable. ... Stem/root tonal types are of three kinds, called H(igh) type, L(ow) type and 0 type.

5203.dq: "बैलगाडी कुठे गेली?" या श्रोत्याच्या प्रश्नाला उत्तर देताना वक्ता 'वावरात' या शब्दावर प्रबल बल देतो. (When answering the listener's question 'Where did the bullock-cart go?' the speaker puts strong stress on the word 'vāvrāt'.) — every stress example is a whole sentence with the stress placed on the word or syllable in focus or contrast.
5203.dloc: Ch. 4 (अ) बल, thesis p. 66, subsections १. प्रबल बल, २. अतिप्रबल बल, ३. तुटक बल, ४. विलंबित बल; read at 200 and (is Latin-font garbage). Intonation/nasalization checked at thesis p. 69 of the same file; vowel-length rule checked at ch. 2 thesis p. 40.
5203.prule: Only emphatic / focus stress is described, at the level of the utterance: 'strong stress' (प्रबल बल) falls on whichever word of the sentence answers the question under discussion (baṇḍi vāvrāt neli: stress on vāvrāt 'to the field' answering 'where?', on baṇḍi 'cart' answering 'what?'); 'extra-strong stress' (अतिप्रबल बल) falls on the particular syllable that carries a contrast (on the ā of āplyā 'our own', not somebody else's); 'clipped stress' (तुटक बल) gives 'only / exactly' readings; 'prolonged stress' (विलंबित बल) marks calls and intensification. No rule for the position of word stress is given, and word stress is neither described nor denied; so the record is phrase-level prominence only, word-level placement unreported.

5205.dq: No sentence: the notebook is a wordlist with no prosodic prose. The marked items are isolated citation forms (single words with English glosses), so the ticks record word-in-isolation stress; the only phrasal items (e.g. p.127 'ia nay kini maləm da' 'he came here yesterday', p.129 'ñən pii'siw' 'don't talk!') are too few to show whether the placement holds in phrase. Blust 2013 sec. 4.1.3 p. 186 …
5205.dloc: Notebook pp. 127, 128, 129, 131, 135 = Kaipuleohone low-res two-page scans RB2-003-A-063 (right page = p.127), -064 (left = p.128, right = p.129), -065 (right = p.131), -067 (right = p.135); Blust 2017 fn. 11 (p. 198).
5205.prule: Final syllable (citation forms). No prose rule in the notebook: the placement is read off Blust's stress tick (ˈ written before the stressed syllable), which in every marked polysyllable on the pages I opened (pp. 127-129, 131, 135; some 200+ forms) precedes the LAST syllable, in disyllables (tu'suʔ, taa'kət, ba'ʔuʔ), trisyllables (kəlu'nan, pəpa'tay, ñəma'yaw, kətən'nəʔ, kəda'yay, jəlu'tuŋ) and the one quadrisyllable (kətəsi'ləp). Long/doubled penultimate vowels (taa-, puu-, sii-) are never the stressed syllable, so the placement is quantity-insensitive. Blust's own published gloss of the same convention for the Western Lowland villages of the same 1971 trip: 'Stress was invariably recorded as final in citation forms' (Blust 2017 fn. 11 p. 198).
5205.srule: Not mentioned in Blust 1971 notebook RB2-003-A, Long Dunin wordlist pp. 127-137 (wordlist with no prosodic prose; every stress-marked citation form carries a single tick before the final syllable; no secondary ticks).

5207.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. The language is described as a three-tone language (high, mid, low) with extensive tone sandhi. Stress appears only (a) as phrase/sentence stress that conditions fast-speech reduction of CVV/CVhV disyllables to one syllable (pp. 8, 54, 61) and (b) as a verb stress that 'shifts from the first syllable to the second' in some imperative forms (p. 43), which presupposes first-syllable stress on bisyllabic verb stems but is not stated as a rule.

5207.exq_: No stress rule is stated, so no exceptions are stated; the only positional remark is itself a shift: "Sometimes the stress of the verb shifts from the first syllable to the second in imperative forms." (p. 43)
5207.tone: Three level tones (high = acute, mid = macron, low = unmarked) with extensive tone sandhi; the sketch writes basic, not surface, tones (p. 8). Stress is named only as 'phrase stress' (pp. 8, 61) / 'sentence stress' (p. 54) blocking fast-speech reduction, as a verb-stress shift first -> second syllable in imperatives (p. 43), and in the labels 'poststressed' / 'prestressed' for clitic pronouns (§5.4, pp. 135–136). Nowhere does the source say where word stress falls. Farris 2004 (dictionary, phonology appendix pp. 139–144: three tones, 'acento' only as the high-tone mark) and Pike 1937 (six-page phonetics of the Mixteca Alta near Chalcatongo, Yucuañe, Yosondúa; only 'emotional stress' and pitch glides) are silent on word stress.
